content.overview: Section 10 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, as substituted by the 2018 amendment, says that the specific performance of a contract shall be enforced by the court, subject to section 11(2), section 14 and section 16. Specific performance is the rule for a contract that survives those sections. It is no longer framed as a discretion to be granted only when damages are inadequate. Sections 14 and 16 are the bars. Section 20 is substituted performance, and obtaining it is itself a section 14 bar.
content.study: Start with section 10, then test sections 14 and 16 before saying the contract shall be enforced. Do not apply the pre-2018 adequacy-of-damages test as the section 10 rule.

learningObjectives: Name the sections that still qualify enforcement.
Keep the old inadequacy test out of section 10.
enhancement.definition: Section 10 requires the court to enforce specific performance of a contract, subject to section 11(2), section 14 and section 16.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Enforcement is mandatory in form, but only if the contract is not one section 14 will not enforce and the plaintiff is not barred by section 16.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: Specific Relief Act, 1963, section 10, as amended in 2018. Sections 11(2), 14 and 16 are the stated qualifications.
essentialIngredients: Enforcement rather than a discretion based on inadequate damages
enhancement.detailedExplanation: The 2018 substitution changed the structure. The court shall enforce specific performance. The subject-to clause points to section 11(2), which deals with a contract made by a trustee in excess of powers or in breach of trust, section 14, which lists contracts that cannot be specifically enforced, and section 16, which lists who cannot obtain specific performance. A plaintiff who has already taken substituted performance under section 20 falls into both the section 14 and section 16 bars. The older teaching that specific performance depends on damages being inadequate is not the text of section 10. Adequacy of money compensation remains relevant to perpetual injunctions under section 38, which is a different remedy.
examples: A sale contract is not determinable, needs no continuous supervision, and the buyer proves readiness. Section 10 says it shall be enforced unless another named section bars it.
The buyer has already had the work done under section 20. Section 10 does not override section 14.
A plaintiff argues only that damages are inadequate. That is not the section 10 test.
enhancement.problemApplication: Identify the contract, then check sections 11(2), 14 and 16. Enforce only if those qualifications are not met.
distinctions: Post-2018 shall-enforce rule vs the old inadequacy discretion
Specific performance vs a section 38 injunction
enhancement.caseLawNotes: No new case citation or ratio was added. Ready-and-willing and adequate-relief readings remain on the case-law gate.
